title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A lawsuit alleges that Otter.ai, an AI transcription service used in virtual meetings, recorded private work conversations without obtaining proper consent from all participants and then used these recordings to train its AI systems. The plaintiff claims he discovered his confidential conversation had been recorded without his knowledge, and the suit contends that Otter's default recording behavior and privacy disclosures violated state and federal privacy laws.

The failure is deployment without adequate consent verification. Otter.ai's software recorded meetings across Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default, yet the system did not ensure all participants affirmatively agreed before recording began. Catching this would have required designing the software to obtain explicit consent from every meeting participant before any recording started, rather than relying on a checkbox in a privacy policy that users may not review.

It is not established whether Otter's anonymization process for training data actually removed identifying information, whether the company's practices technically violated applicable law, or what consequences, if any, will result from the lawsuit.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service used for virtual meetings, of secretly recording private work conversations without proper consent. The suit claims that Otter's software, which transcribes Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings, records discussions by default without asking all participants for permission and then uses these recordings to train its AI systems for financial gain. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was severely violated when he discovered Otter had recorded a confidential conversation. The lawsuit contends that Otter's practices violate state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

The case highlights growing privacy concerns about Otter, which has 25 million users and has recorded over 1 billion meetings since 2016. Users have reported troubling incidents, including an investor meeting where confidential details were transcribed and shared, damaging a business deal. The lawsuit argues that while Otter's privacy policy mentions getting permission through a checkbox, many users are still being deceived. Additionally, the suit questions whether Otter's process for anonymizing data before using it for AI training actually removes confidential information and guarantees speaker anonymity.
